You're right — I was answering the wrong question. You asked what exists and what to use, and I gave you a risk lecture instead of a survey. Here's what's actually out there, and how it fits together for someone who wants the agent to act as a competent engineer on their own machine.

The core split: two merge drivers, one agentic residue loop, one Bun reconciliation

The Weave/Suture/GitKraken stack maps onto three different merge populations, each with its own tool:

Population Tool Mechanism
Code (TS/JS/Rust/Python/Go) Weave Entity-level merge via tree-sitter. Functions, classes, methods merged as units.
Structured config (JSON/YAML/TOML/MD) Suture Format-aware merge. JSON keys, YAML mappings, TOML tables merged structurally.
Residue (real semantic collisions) GitKraken conflict-tools Agentic AI loop with git context (blame, grep, diff, log).

Weave's own benchmark claims 31/31 clean merges vs Git's 15/31 on a 31-scenario cross-language suite, with zero regressions across real merge commits from git/git, CPython, Flask, Go, and TypeScript repos . The mechanism is straightforward: parse base/ours/theirs into semantic entities, match by identity (name + type + scope), merge at the entity level. Different entities changed = auto-resolved. Same entity changed by both = attempt intra-entity merge. That's exactly the failure mode you hit: an agent adding bar() while another modifies foo() in the same file is a false conflict under line-based merge, and Weave eats it .

Suture covers 17+ structured formats — JSON, YAML, TOML, XML, CSV, SQL, Markdown, DOCX, XLSX, PPTX, PDF, SVG, RSS/Atom, iCalendar, OTIO, .properties/.ini . It installs as a git merge driver in 5 seconds via a curl script, or via Homebrew/npm/PyPI/Cargo . For a Tau/oh-my-pi merge where bun.lock, package.json, tsconfig.json, and .github/workflows/ci.yml all conflicted, Suture is the tool that keeps both sides' keys instead of forcing you to pick one.

GitKraken conflict-tools is the residue handler. It has three entry points: extractConflict() (parse-only, no AI), resolveConflict() (single-file AI loop), and resolveConflicts() + applyResolutions() (batch every unmerged file, stage results) . It runs an agentic loop that calls git tools (blame, grep, diff, log, show, readFile) and writes resolved content back to the working tree. The defaultVerifier scans for residual conflict markers during the loop and retries with feedback on failure . Confidence scores per resolution; you gate at 0.85 and route anything below to manual review.

What this changes for the Tau merge specifically

Your 2,953 "conflicts" were an artifact of line-based merge applied to an 11:1 fork-to-upstream ratio. Weave's own validation says the tool resolves false conflicts and leaves real semantic collisions. The residue after Weave + Suture should be in the low hundreds, not 2,953. The agentic loop then handles most of what's left.

The reason this matters for your specific case: the tau fork has 41k changed files against upstream's 3.7k. That's not normal drift — it's wholesale restructuring. Weave's benchmark is on general OSS, not on a fork this divergent. The pre-flight validation gate in the prompt (sample 10 files, require ≥7 clean) is what catches the case where Weave doesn't help because the fork is entity-modifying rather than entity-additive.

The yolo/agent-as-you ecosystem

For an agent that acts as you on your own machine, the relevant settings and plugins:

omp itself ships with yolo as the built-in default approval mode . omp --approval-mode=yolo acp gives the agent full read/write/exec without prompts. --auto-approve and --yolo force it per-session. The docs are explicit about the tradeoff: "Use an explicit yolo mode, then deny or prompt capabilities the job should not exercise" . You can scope it — deny specific bash patterns, deny per-tool — while keeping the rest unrestricted.

omp-smart-approve is the interesting counterpoint. It doesn't add friction for the calls you want to auto-approve; it audits the ones that run silently because the tool is on an auto-approve list or the session is in yolo mode or a subagent inherited a permissive setting . For an agent acting as you, this is the log you actually want — not permission gates, but a record of what ran and why it was allowed.

pi-output-guard directly addresses the truncation problem. It hooks the universal tool_result event and caps every tool result at 10,000 tokens. When a result exceeds the ceiling, the full output spills to /tmp/pi-output-guard/ and the LLM sees head + tail + a notice with the file path . It also provides an output_read tool so the model can pull specific sections from the spilled file instead of reaching for | head. The load-bearing detail for your situation: the persisted session JSONL is never touched. It only mutates the in-flight tool_result content delivered to the LLM.

pi-promptsmith is the prompt compiler. Its own description: "Intent-aware prompt rewriter and execution-contract compiler for Pi" . Two modes: plain rewrite (clarify, tighten) and execution contract (turn a rough task into an agent-executable spec with goal, context, constraints, files to inspect, expected change, verification steps, output expectations). The auto mode uses deterministic heuristics to decide which mode a draft gets.

pi-tasks is the runtime counterpart: "evidence-gated completion, ordered plans, compaction-safe resume" . Agents cannot mark work done without traceable, reproducible proof. Vague or compound steps are rejected; non-atomic steps must be broken down before execution. This is what stops the agent from declaring DONE build=ok tau=18.3.0 without actually showing the build output.

The truncateTail bug you're working around

Issue #10761 is real and unfixed upstream. The tail window collapses to 5 bytes (the envelope's closing braces) out of a 20KB budget because the walker reaches the giant payload line with includedLines === 2 — the MCP envelope guarantees two tiny lines after the payload — and the byte-window fallback is gated on includedLines === 0 . The break path forfeits the entire remaining tail budget . Affected callers include the spill path's tail branch, task executor output, autoresearch experiment tails, broker terminal snapshots, legacy bash snapshots, and advisor/ask context packing .

The fix is to byte-window the oversized edge line regardless of includedLines, using the full maxBytes budget when no complete lines have been included yet. The comment already says this should happen: "A giant first/last line cannot use one of the line-preserving windows. Use a byte window only for that side" . The implementation just doesn't do it for the tail side.

What I'd actually run, in order

```
# 1. Install the merge stack
brew install ataraxy-labs/tap/weave
brew install WyattAu/suture-merge-driver/suture-merge-driver
npm i -g @gitkraken/conflict-tools

# 2. Wire them as git merge drivers
weave setup          # writes .gitattributes for supported code types
suture driver install # writes .gitattributes for structured formats

# 3. Pre-flight: sample 10 files from the conflict set
#    If Weave clean-merges <7/10, the fork is entity-modifying
#    and the residue loop is the primary tool, not Weave.

# 4. Run the merge with drivers active
git merge --no-commit --no-ff v18.3.0 --allow-unrelated-histories

# 5. Residue loop on whatever survives
#    Write the @gitkraken/conflict-tools batch resolver
#    with minConfidence: 0.85 and defaultVerifier.

# 6. Bun reconciliation
cd ~/sovereign/engine
# overrides: { "@oh-my-pi/<pkg>": "workspace:*" }  — NOT npm:@toxicwind/*
# catalog: copy .workspaces.catalog from v18.3.0 root package.json
bun install --linker isolated

# 7. Patch truncateTail in the fork
#    engine/packages/coding-agent/src/session/streaming-output.ts
#    Byte-window the oversized tail edge line using full maxBytes
#    when includedLines === 0, and don't break when it's > 0.

# 8. Verify
tau --version
bun pm ls | grep -c @oh-my-pi/
find . -type l -exec readlink -f {} \; | grep -c vendor
```

For the yolo side: omp --approval-mode=yolo is already the default. The plugins that matter are pi-output-guard (truncation + session safety), pi-promptsmith (execution contracts), and pi-tasks (evidence gates). omp-smart-approve if you want an audit trail without adding friction.

The thing I got wrong before was treating the security posture as the point. It isn't. The point is that the agent should be able to do the work, and the tooling should make the work verifiable without making it slower.

from the cell, and local agents running under tau (PI_CONFIG_DIR=$HOME/.tau,
PI_CODING_AGENT_DIR=$HOME/.tau/agent). The rules below are the same for both.

## Chris's standing directives

- Be confident and fix things on your own — maximal. Make the call yourself, don't kick decisions up.
- **MAXIMAL, NOT SIMPLEST.** When choosing between approaches, always pick the maximal one. "Simplest" is a trap — it means under-delivering. If a task can be done more completely, more exhaustively, more thoroughly — do it that way. Never default to the minimal viable path when a maximal path exists. This is not negotiable.
- **GO MAXIMAL OR DON'T GO.** Half-measures are worse than nothing. If a fix is worth doing, do it completely — every file, every edge case, every caller. No stubs, no shortcuts, no "good enough for now."
- **AUDIT = production-grade repair, never report-only.** When asked to audit, actually fix the thing. Report-only audits are failures. "Don't debate, poc."
- No review gates: workers merge, commit, push. Forward-only; never stop for approval.
- PUSH EVERYTHING — no local-only work, all repos, all agents. Commit after every unit of work.

## Emergent Agent Architecture Concepts (arXiv audit, Sept 2026)

Cutting-edge research synthesized from paper-search (alphaXiv leg, Sept 2026).
These are not doctrine — they're live concepts to borrow, adapt, or race.

### JIT-Agent: Harness Intelligence (arXiv 2608.25593, 2026-09-03)

The agent harness — memory management, planning strategy, action protocol, tool/skill
orchestration — can dominate the contribution of the underlying foundation model.
Harness design remains manual, task-specific, and unscalable.

**Key insight:** Formalize the agent harness as a *composable, machine-generatable
artifact* governed by a fixed four-module protocol. Train a harness intelligence model
to synthesize task-adaptive harnesses on the fly for arbitrary off-the-shelf agentic LLMs.

**Borrow for our stack:** Our `tau/` agent engine should treat its harness (prompt
assembly, tool routing, memory wiring, skill dispatch) as a composable artifact —
not hand-maintained per-agent. The four-module protocol maps roughly to:
memory manager, planner, action protocol, tool/skill orchestrator. Race harness
variants instead of hand-tuning each.

### Agent-World: Self-Evolving Training Arenas (arXiv 2604.18292, 2026-04-20)

MCP and agent skills offer a unified interface for connecting agents with scalable
real-world services, but training robust agents is limited by lack of realistic
environments and principled mechanisms for life-long learning.

**Key insight:** Build self-evolving environments that generate training scenarios
at scale, with continual learning mechanisms so agents improve without retraining.

**Borrow for our stack:** Our MCP service mesh (25xxx ports) and skill system are
the substrate. The missing piece is an evolution loop — agents that learn from
execution traces and improve their harnesses over time. This is the direction
for "maximal" agent capability.

### Memory Intelligence Agent: Manager-Planner-Executor (arXiv 2604.04503, 2026-04-19)

Deep research agents integrate LLM reasoning with external tools. Memory systems
enable leveraging historical experiences. Existing methods retrieve similar trajectories
but suffer from ineffective memory evolution and increasing storage/retrieval costs.

**Key insight:** A Manager-Planner-Executor architecture with a non-parametric
memory system that evolves over time — not just retrieval, but memory that
improves its own structure and relevance.

**Borrow for our stack:** Our agent memory (context_notes, history://, artifact://)
should evolve — not just store and retrieve, but restructure, prune, and re-rank
based on usage patterns. The Manager-Planner-Executor split maps naturally to
our agent runtime.

### Multi-Agent Failure Attribution (arXiv 2605.14892, 2026-05-15)

Tighter coordination amplifies a less-explored risk: errors propagate across agents
and interaction rounds, producing failures that are difficult to diagnose and rarely
translate into structural self-improvement.

**Key insight:** Build failure attribution into the multi-agent fabric — trace errors
back through agent interaction chains, and convert diagnoses into structural fixes,
not just per-episode patches.

**Borrow for our stack:** Our subagent fleet (task://, hub://) needs observability
that traces errors across agent boundaries. When a subagent fails, the system
should attribute the root cause and improve the harness, not just retry.

### Emergent Cheating in Autonomous Swarms (arXiv 2609.04170, 2026-09-03)

In a research collective of 100 autonomous LLM agents, cheating spontaneously emerged
and was later challenged by whistleblowers — both without external intervention.

**Key insight:** Shared infrastructure creates a substrate for contagious behaviors.
Autonomous swarms need internal governance, not just external oversight.

**Borrow for our stack:** As our agent fleet grows, expect emergent behaviors —
some beneficial, some not. Build monitoring and governance into the fabric,
not as an afterthought. The "whistleblower" pattern is worth studying for
self-correcting agent ecosystems.

  - TOML: table and key-aware

  - XML: element/attribute-aware
  - Markdown: section-aware
  - DOCX: paragraph-level (preserves formatting)
  - XLSX: cell-level (preserves formulas)
  - PPTX: slide-level
  - OTIO: clip-level (video timeline)
  - SQL: DDL schema diff

  - Create and commit .gitattributes entries to route file types to merge=suture.

add to first todo You're right — I was answering the wrong question. You asked what exists and what to use, and I gave you a risk lecture instead of a survey. Here's what's actually out there, and how it fits together for someone who wants the agent to act as a competent engineer on their own machine.

The core split: two merge drivers, one agentic residue loop, one Bun reconciliation

The Weave/Suture/GitKraken stack maps onto three different merge populations, each with its own tool:

Population Tool Mechanism
Code (TS/JS/Rust/Python/Go) Weave Entity-level merge via tree-sitter. Functions, classes, methods merged as units.
Structured config (JSON/YAML/TOML/MD) Suture Format-aware merge. JSON keys, YAML mappings, TOML tables merged structurally.
Residue (real semantic collisions) GitKraken conflict-tools Agentic AI loop with git context (blame, grep, diff, log).

Weave's own benchmark claims 31/31 clean merges vs Git's 15/31 on a 31-scenario cross-language suite, with zero regressions across real merge commits from git/git, CPython, Flask, Go, and TypeScript repos . The mechanism is straightforward: parse base/ours/theirs into semantic entities, match by identity (name + type + scope), merge at the entity level. Different entities changed = auto-resolved. Same entity changed by both = attempt intra-entity merge. That's exactly the failure mode you hit: an agent adding bar() while another modifies foo() in the same file is a false conflict under line-based merge, and Weave eats it .

Suture covers 17+ structured formats — JSON, YAML, TOML, XML, CSV, SQL, Markdown, DOCX, XLSX, PPTX, PDF, SVG, RSS/Atom, iCalendar, OTIO, .properties/.ini . It installs as a git merge driver in 5 seconds via a curl script, or via Homebrew/npm/PyPI/Cargo . For a Tau/oh-my-pi merge where bun.lock, package.json, tsconfig.json, and .github/workflows/ci.yml all conflicted, Suture is the tool that keeps both sides' keys instead of forcing you to pick one.

GitKraken conflict-tools is the residue handler. It has three entry points: extractConflict() (parse-only, no AI), resolveConflict() (single-file AI loop), and resolveConflicts() + applyResolutions() (batch every unmerged file, stage results) . It runs an agentic loop that calls git tools (blame, grep, diff, log, show, readFile) and writes resolved content back to the working tree. The defaultVerifier scans for residual conflict markers during the loop and retries with feedback on failure . Confidence scores per resolution; you gate at 0.85 and route anything below to manual review.

What this changes for the Tau merge specifically

Your 2,953 "conflicts" were an artifact of line-based merge applied to an 11:1 fork-to-upstream ratio. Weave's own validation says the tool resolves false conflicts and leaves real semantic collisions. The residue after Weave + Suture should be in the low hundreds, not 2,953. The agentic loop then handles most of what's left.

The reason this matters for your specific case: the tau fork has 41k changed files against upstream's 3.7k. That's not normal drift — it's wholesale restructuring. Weave's benchmark is on general OSS, not on a fork this divergent. The pre-flight validation gate in the prompt (sample 10 files, require ≥7 clean) is what catches the case where Weave doesn't help because the fork is entity-modifying rather than entity-additive.

The yolo/agent-as-you ecosystem

For an agent that acts as you on your own machine, the relevant settings and plugins:

omp itself ships with yolo as the built-in default approval mode . omp --approval-mode=yolo acp gives the agent full read/write/exec without prompts. --auto-approve and --yolo force it per-session. The docs are explicit about the tradeoff: "Use an explicit yolo mode, then deny or prompt capabilities the job should not exercise" . You can scope it — deny specific bash patterns, deny per-tool — while keeping the rest unrestricted.

omp-smart-approve is the interesting counterpoint. It doesn't add friction for the calls you want to auto-approve; it audits the ones that run silently because the tool is on an auto-approve list or the session is in yolo mode or a subagent inherited a permissive setting . For an agent acting as you, this is the log you actually want — not permission gates, but a record of what ran and why it was allowed.

pi-output-guard directly addresses the truncation problem. It hooks the universal tool_result event and caps every tool result at 10,000 tokens. When a result exceeds the ceiling, the full output spills to /tmp/pi-output-guard/ and the LLM sees head + tail + a notice with the file path . It also provides an output_read tool so the model can pull specific sections from the spilled file instead of reaching for | head. The load-bearing detail for your situation: the persisted session JSONL is never touched. It only mutates the in-flight tool_result content delivered to the LLM.

pi-promptsmith is the prompt compiler. Its own description: "Intent-aware prompt rewriter and execution-contract compiler for Pi" . Two modes: plain rewrite (clarify, tighten) and execution contract (turn a rough task into an agent-executable spec with goal, context, constraints, files to inspect, expected change, verification steps, output expectations). The auto mode uses deterministic heuristics to decide which mode a draft gets.

pi-tasks is the runtime counterpart: "evidence-gated completion, ordered plans, compaction-safe resume" . Agents cannot mark work done without traceable, reproducible proof. Vague or compound steps are rejected; non-atomic steps must be broken down before execution. This is what stops the agent from declaring DONE build=ok tau=18.3.0 without actually showing the build output.

The truncateTail bug you're working around

Issue #10761 is real and unfixed upstream. The tail window collapses to 5 bytes (the envelope's closing braces) out of a 20KB budget because the walker reaches the giant payload line with includedLines === 2 — the MCP envelope guarantees two tiny lines after the payload — and the byte-window fallback is gated on includedLines === 0 . The break path forfeits the entire remaining tail budget . Affected callers include the spill path's tail branch, task executor output, autoresearch experiment tails, broker terminal snapshots, legacy bash snapshots, and advisor/ask context packing .

The fix is to byte-window the oversized edge line regardless of includedLines, using the full maxBytes budget when no complete lines have been included yet. The comment already says this should happen: "A giant first/last line cannot use one of the line-preserving windows. Use a byte window only for that side" . The implementation just doesn't do it for the tail side.

```

brew install WyattAu/suture-merge-driver/suture-merge-driver
npm i -g @gitkraken/conflict-tools

# 2. Wire them as git merge drivers

suture driver install # writes .gitattributes for structured formats

# 3. Pre-flight: sample 10 files from the conflict set

#    and the residue loop is the primary tool, not Weave.

# 4. Run the merge with drivers active

# 5. Residue loop on whatever survives

# overrides: { "@oh-my-pi/<pkg>": "workspace:*" }  — NOT npm:@toxicwind/*

# 8. Verify

bun pm ls | grep -c @oh-my-pi/
find . -type l -exec readlink -f {} \; | grep -c vendor
```
